opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is data. The internet's natural data is finite, and much of the high-quality part has already been used. For AI to keep improving, you need a way to produce new, useful signal, and that is where a world model becomes important.

If you have a good world model, a model that can predict how an environment responds to actions, then you can let the AI explore, try things, and get feedback inside that model without a human labeling every step. In an AI-training-AI loop, one model proposes tasks or actions, the world model simulates the consequences, and another model, or the same one, learns from the outcomes. So the world model becomes a kind of engine for data. It turns compute into experience.

For generalization, what matters is coverage and diversity. When you train only on static human data, the model learns the distribution people happened to write down. A world model lets you go into regions people never recorded: long-horizon tasks, rare situations, counterfactuals like "what if I had done this differently." If the world model is accurate enough, training on those trajectories helps the policy learn the underlying structure rather than surface patterns, and that kind of learning is what transfers.

There's a catch, of course. If the world model is wrong, the agent will exploit its errors, the reward-hacking problem. So the world model has to be grounded and verifiable. That's why I think the most promising areas right now are ones with reliable feedback, like code, math, and tool use, where you can check results against reality. Over time you expand from these verifiable domains to fuzzier ones as the world model improves.

So I'd put it this way: pretraining gave us a good prior about the world, and reinforcement learning with a world model is how you scale beyond what humans have written down. The two together are, I think, the main path to stronger generalization from here.

r001.rationale: The response explains that an accurate world model can simulate actions and outcomes for AI training, generating diverse experience that can help the policy learn underlying structure and generalize.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that when people talk about "AI training AI," there are really two different things being mixed together. One is AI generating data for another model to learn from. The other is AI providing the signal, the reward, the judgment about whether something was done well. World models are relevant to both, but I think they matter more for the second one, and that's where the generalization story gets interesting.

The reason RL today works so well on math and code is that you have a verifier. The answer is right or wrong, the tests pass or they don't. The environment itself is the world model, in a sense. It's a perfect simulator of the consequences of your actions. So the model can explore, make mistakes, get feedback, and that loop runs millions of times without a human in it. That's why we see such fast progress in those domains.

But most of the world doesn't come with a verifier. If you write a research proposal, if you negotiate with someone, if you plan a trip, if you run a long agent task across many tools, there is no function that returns zero or one. So the question is: can the model itself learn a good enough model of how the world responds, so that it can serve as the environment for its own training? That's what I mean by world model in this context. Not necessarily video prediction, but a model that can predict consequences, including consequences in text, in software, in human reactions.

If you have that, then generalization improves for a fairly simple reason. Right now, when we do RL on a narrow domain, the model gets very good at the surface statistics of that domain's reward. It overfits to the verifier. A world model gives you a much broader reward surface, because it's modeling the actual dynamics rather than one task's checker. The model has to learn things that are true across tasks, not just things that are rewarded in one task. And the data you generate from it is more diverse, because you're not sampling from a fixed set of problems, you're rolling out trajectories in a space that the world model can extend.

There's a second effect that I think is underrated. A good world model lets you do something like planning before you act. The policy proposes, the world model predicts, and you can select or revise before you commit. That's a form of test-time compute, but it's grounded in prediction rather than just longer chains of thought. And training on those improved trajectories feeds back into the policy. So you get a loop where the policy gets better because the world model is good, and the world model gets better because the policy explores more interesting states. The two co-evolve.

Now, the honest caveat is that this only works if the world model is actually accurate in the places that matter. If it's wrong, the policy learns to exploit the errors, and you get the classic problem of optimizing against a flawed simulator. The model becomes very good at fooling its own world model. So a lot of the real engineering work is about keeping the world model anchored to reality: mixing in real environment feedback, real user outcomes, real execution results, so that the synthetic loop doesn't drift. I don't think you can ever go fully closed-loop. You need some contact with the ground truth.

But I'm fairly optimistic about the direction. If you look at the history, pretraining was about compressing the world's data. RL with verifiers was about learning from consequences in domains where consequences are cheap to compute. World models are the natural next step: making consequences cheap to compute everywhere, by learning them. And once that happens, the amount of useful experience a model can generate is no longer bounded by what humans wrote down or what we can hand-build verifiers for. That's where I think the real jump in generalization will come from.

r001.rationale: The response says a sufficiently accurate world model could predict how the world responds and serve as an environment for training, generating broader experience that can improve generalization.

astra-6.text:
I think world models could help by giving AI a way to explore the consequences of its actions, rather than just learning from a fixed set of examples. In an AI-training-AI setup, you could use a world model to generate situations, test different strategies, and provide feedback to another model.

For generalization, the important question is whether those situations introduce meaningful variation. Can you change the environment or the constraints and still learn principles that carry over? If so, the training process can go beyond reproducing patterns in the original data.

But there’s a limitation: the world model can be wrong, and the model being trained can learn to exploit those errors. So I’d see this as a loop between simulated experience and real-world feedback. The world model lets you explore more broadly, while external feedback keeps that exploration grounded.

r001.rationale: The response says a world model can generate situations and test strategies in an AI-training-AI setup, with meaningful variation and transferable principles improving generalization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think world models can provide a way to train on consequences, rather than just imitate existing answers. If a model can take an action, predict how the environment changes, and then check whether that prediction was correct, you get a much richer learning signal.

In an AI-training-AI setup, that could let us generate tasks and interactions where another model learns to plan, explore, and recover from mistakes. The hope is that it learns underlying rules that transfer to new situations, instead of memorizing particular solutions.

But the important question is how we ground that process. If the world model has a systematic error, the model training inside it may learn to exploit that error. So generating more synthetic experience is not sufficient by itself. We need feedback from real environments, or outcomes we can reliably verify, to keep the training useful. I see world models as a promising way to scale interactive experience, with grounding as a key condition for better generalization.

r001.rationale: The response describes using a world model to simulate actions and their consequences, then train another model through generated interactions so it learns rules that transfer to new situations. It presents this as a promising route to better generalization in AI-training-AI.
